paragraphs.text:
[calm] Outside, the night was cold and wet. But inside the small parlour of Laburnam Villa, the fire burned brightly and the room was warm. Mr. White and his son Herbert were playing chess, while Mrs. White sat knitting quietly by the fire.

Mr. White liked to take chances at chess. He saw too late that he had left his king in danger. "Listen to the wind," he said, hoping to distract his son.

"I can hear it," said Herbert. "Check."

"I don't suppose he'll come tonight," said his father, his hand still over the board.

"Checkmate."

Mr. White suddenly raised his voice. This was what came of living so far out! The path was all mud and the road was like a river. Mrs. White told him he might win the next game. He caught the look she and Herbert shared, and hid a smile in his beard.

The gate banged and heavy footsteps came up the path. Mr. White hurried to the door and brought in their guest, Sergeant-Major Morris, an old soldier who had spent twenty-one years in India.

He sat down by the fire. By his third glass of whiskey he was telling them about wars, deadly diseases and the people he had met far from home. The family listened with great interest. Mr. White said he would like to go to India himself and see the old temples.

"You're better off here," said Morris.

"What was that you started to tell me the other day about a monkey's paw?"

"Oh, nothing worth telling," said Morris quickly. Mrs. White leaned forward. Now she wanted to hear it too.

[nervous] Morris reached into his pocket and held out a little paw, dry and withered. Mrs. White drew back, but Herbert took it and looked at it closely. His father took it from him and laid it on the table.

"A holy man in India put a spell on it," Morris said. "He wanted to show that fate rules our lives. If we try to change it, we'll be sorry. Three men can each make three wishes with it."

The family laughed a little, but Morris was so serious that the laughter died away.

"Why don't you make three wishes, then?" asked Herbert.

"I already have," said Morris. His face went pale.

"And did they really come true?" asked Mrs. White. Morris said they had. His glass tapped against his teeth.

"The first man who had it made three wishes," he went on. "I don't know what the first two were. His third wish was for death. That is how I got the paw."

A silence fell over the room. Mr. White asked why Morris still kept it. He had thought of selling it, Morris said, but it had already caused enough trouble. Some people thought it was a fairy tale, and the rest wanted to try it before paying. Would he make those wishes again if he could? Morris said he didn't know.

Then, without warning, he threw the paw onto the fire. Mr. White snatched it back. "If you don't want it," he said, "give it to me."

Morris refused. He had thrown it away, and if Mr. White kept it, he must take the blame for whatever happened. But Mr. White was already asking how to use it. Morris told him to hold it up in his right hand and make his wish aloud.

As Mrs. White got supper ready, she joked that he could wish for four pairs of hands for her. Mr. White reached for the paw, and Morris caught him by the arm. The others laughed. If he had to wish for something, Morris told him, it had better be something sensible.

They ate and listened to more stories about India. Once Morris had left to catch the last train, Herbert joked about Morris's stories. If the one about the paw was as true as the rest, they wouldn't get much from it. Mr. White admitted that he had paid a little for it. Morris had only taken the money because Mr. White insisted, and he had told him again to throw it away.

Herbert suggested that his father wish to be an emperor, so his mother couldn't tell him what to do. She grabbed a cloth from a chair and chased him round the table. Mr. White looked at the paw. He seemed to have everything he wanted already.

"Two hundred pounds would pay off what you owe on the house," Herbert said, putting a hand on his father's shoulder. "Wish for that."

Herbert sat down at the piano, winked at his mother and played a few solemn chords. Mr. White felt a little foolish as he held up the paw in his right hand. "I wish for two hundred pounds."

[sigh] Herbert struck a loud chord as his father spoke. Mr. White cried out, and they both ran to him. The paw lay on the floor.

"It moved," said Mr. White. He said it had twisted in his hand like a snake.

Herbert put it back on the table. "I don't see any money," he said. Mrs. White told her husband that he must have imagined it, though she watched him anxiously. He shook his head. It had given him a fright, he said, but there was no harm done.

The wind was stronger now. At the sound of a door banging upstairs, Mr. White jumped. They sat by the fire in an uneasy silence until the old couple went to bed. Herbert joked that they would find a bag of money in the middle of the bed and something horrible watching them from the top of the wardrobe.

Alone in the dark, he watched faces form in the dying fire. The last face looked so horribly like a monkey that he reached for a glass of water to throw on the coals. His hand closed around the paw instead. He shivered, wiped his hand on his coat and went to bed.

In the morning the winter sun shone on the breakfast table, and Herbert laughed at how frightened he had been. The withered paw had been tossed onto the sideboard. Mrs. White called the story nonsense. Even if wishes could come true, how could two hundred pounds hurt anyone?

"They might fall on his head," said Herbert. Mr. White said Morris had warned him that things would happen so naturally that they could pass for a coincidence. Herbert told his father not to spend the money before he came home, and his mother laughed as she watched him walk down the road to work. All the same, she hurried to the door when the postman knocked. He had only brought a bill from the tailor.

At dinner, Mr. White was still insisting that the paw had moved when his wife noticed a well-dressed man in a shiny silk hat. He stopped three times at the gate and walked on. The fourth time he opened it. Mrs. White hid her apron under the cushion of her chair before she let him in.

The visitor seemed ill at ease. He picked a loose thread from his trousers. At last he said that he had come from Maw and Meggins, where Herbert worked. Mrs. White asked if something had happened to her son. Her husband tried to calm her.

"Is he hurt?" she asked.

"Very badly," said the visitor, "but he isn't in pain."

Mrs. White started to thank God. Then she saw the man's face and fell silent. Her hand was trembling as she laid it on her husband's.

"He was caught in the machinery," the visitor said at last.

Mr. White repeated the words slowly. He held his wife's hand the way he used to when they were young. Herbert was the only one they had left.

The visitor went to the window. The company sent its sympathy, he said. He asked them to remember that he was only doing his job. Maw and Meggins accepted no responsibility for the accident. But in recognition of Herbert's work, they wanted to offer the family some money as compensation.

[whispers] Mr. White let go of his wife's hand and stood up. "How much?"

"Two hundred pounds," said the man.

Mrs. White screamed, but her husband didn't seem to hear her. He gave a faint smile. He stretched out his hands as if he couldn't see, and collapsed.

They buried Herbert in the new cemetery, two miles away, and returned to a house full of shadows and silence. At first they felt as if they were waiting for something else to happen, something that would make their loss easier to bear. Then the days went by, and sometimes they hardly spoke at all.

About a week after the funeral, Mr. White woke in the dark and found his wife was not beside him. She was crying at the window. He asked her to come back to bed before she got cold.

"It's colder for my son," she said.

He fell asleep again, then woke to a cry. Mrs. White hurried over to him. "The paw! You haven't thrown it away?"

He told her it was on the shelf by the fireplace. She laughed and cried at once, and kissed his cheek.

"We still have two wishes," she said. "Go and get it. Wish for our boy to be alive again."

Mr. White sat up in horror. He struck a match and lit the candle. His wife said that the first wish had come true. Why shouldn't the second?

"A coincidence," he said, his voice shaking. "He's been dead ten days. I only knew it was him by his clothes. It was too terrible for you to see him then. Think what it would be like now."

"Bring him back," she cried, pulling him towards the door. "Do you think I'm afraid of the child I raised?"

[nervous] He went downstairs alone and felt his way through the dark parlour to the fireplace. The paw was still on the mantelpiece, the shelf just above the fire. He was suddenly afraid that even the wish he hadn't spoken might bring Herbert into the room before he could get out. His forehead was cold with sweat. He felt his way around the table and along the wall until he found the door.

Back upstairs, his wife was waiting. To him, even her face looked strange. He was afraid of her.

"Wish!" she cried.

He said it was wrong, but she told him again to wish. He raised his hand. "I wish my son alive again."

The paw fell to the floor. Mr. White sank into a chair while his wife raised the blind and looked out of the window. The candle threw moving shadows on the walls. At last it flickered and went out. Mr. White went back to bed, relieved. A minute or two later his wife lay down beside him. Neither of them spoke.

They listened to the clock ticking. A stair creaked and a mouse ran behind the wall. Mr. White struck a match and went downstairs to fetch another candle. At the bottom of the stairs the match went out. As he stopped to strike another, there was a knock at the front door, so soft that he could hardly hear it.

The matches fell from his hand. He stood still until the knock came again. Then he ran back to the bedroom and shut the door. There was a third knock.

"What's that?" cried Mrs. White.

"A rat," he said. "It ran past me on the stairs."

The next knock shook the house. "It's Herbert!" she cried. He caught her by the arm before she could leave the room.

"I forgot how far away the cemetery was. Let me go!"

"Please, don't let it in," he begged.

"You're afraid of your own son," she said. "I'm coming, Herbert!"

[tense silence] Another knock came, and then another. Mrs. White pulled free and ran downstairs. Her husband heard her take off the chain and slide back the bolt at the bottom of the door.

"The top bolt!" she cried. "Come down. I can't reach it."

On his hands and knees, Mr. White felt along the floor for the paw with trembling hands. If only he could find it before whatever was outside got in. The knocking grew louder. He heard a chair scrape as his wife pushed it against the door. The bolt creaked as she slid it back. His fingers closed around the paw, and he breathed his third and last wish.

The knocking stopped. Its echoes were still in the house when he heard the chair move back and the door open. A cold wind rushed up the stairs. At his wife's cry of disappointment and misery, he found the courage to go down to her, then out to the gate. Across the road a street lamp flickered. The road was quiet and deserted.

quizzes.question: What did the holy man in India put on the monkey's paw?
options: A spell that allows three men to make three wishes each.
A spell that lets three men share a total of three wishes.
A spell that grants one man a new wish every time he holds it.

quizzes.question: Why did the amount of compensation shock Mr. White?
options: It was the amount he still owed the company.
It was exactly the amount he had wished for.
It was the amount the visitor said Herbert had earned that year.
